segments.text: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Sam from Curbside Lunch Club, and today is about how we price office lunch.
Quick housekeeping first. The recording will be sent out after, and there's a Q&A at the end.
Okay. So as I said in the intro email, we run street food lunch for offices, twice a week.
Let me share my screen. Can everyone see the slide? Great.
So this slide is our first price sheet from last spring. Ignore the colors.
Here's the mistake almost every food business makes. You price for your first customer, the friendly one who'd pay anything.
But you should price for your last customer, the office manager who has ten other options and a budget spreadsheet.
If the price works for her, it works for everyone. If it only works for your best fan, you don't have a business, you have a favor.
We started at nine dollars a person, with a twenty person minimum.
And honestly, the minimum mattered more than the price.
Below twenty people, the drive across town eats the margin. Above twenty, the route pays for itself.
So the first thing I'd tell you: find the number that makes the trip worth it, and make that your minimum.
Um, let me go back a slide. Sorry. Okay, this one.
Now, the second thing. People always ask, should I offer a discount to get the first offices in.
I did. It was a mistake.
Every office I got with a discount asked for the discount again. Every single one.
The offices that paid full price from day one never once asked. Not once.
A discount doesn't just lower your price. It tells them what kind of customer to be.
So instead of a discount, we gave a free first lunch for the office manager and two coworkers. Three meals.
That cost us about twenty seven dollars in food, and it closed more offices than the discount ever did.
Okay, I see a question in the chat. Someone asks about tipping. We'll get to that in the Q&A.
Third thing, and this is the one I wish someone had told me. Raise your price before you need to.
We waited until costs went up, and then the raise felt like an emergency, and it sounded like one in the email.
The next time, we raised by one dollar, gave sixty days notice, and added a second sauce option at the same time.
Nobody left. Two offices actually wrote back to say thanks for the notice.
Short notice feels like a bill. Long notice feels like respect.
Alright, let me check the time. We have about eight minutes left, so let's do questions.
First question: how do you find offices to pitch? Honestly, we walk the route at eleven thirty and look for people carrying sad sandwiches.
That sounds like a joke, but it's our best lead source. If people are leaving the building to eat, there's demand.
Second question: what about dietary needs? We always have one vegan dish and we label the big allergens. That covers most offices.
Third question, about tipping. We don't ask for tips on office orders. The price is the price. It keeps the invoice simple for the office manager.
Next question: would I do a subscription instead of per order? We're testing it with two offices now, so ask me again in three months.
Okay, I think that's it. Thanks so much for coming. If you want the price sheet template, it's in the follow-up email.
Bye everyone.
